screens.title: Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing Basics
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on two complementary practices that keep systems safe: vulnerability scanning and penetration testing. Vulnerability scanning is an automated sweep that compares hosts and services against a database of known issues so you can detect problems broadly and regularly. Penetration testing is an intentional, often manual, simulated attack that tries to exploit weaknesses to measure real-world impact. You will also learn core network discovery techniques with Nmap, and how to interpret a simulated OpenVAS, now Greenbone GVM, scan report. We will practice reading CVSS severity, prioritizing fixes, and documenting the scan-remediate-verify cycle. Importantly, we’ll cover the ethical and legal constraints that govern testing so you never scan without explicit written permission. By the end of this chapter you will know which tool to apply for which goal, how to run safe, sensible scans, and how to act on the results. Consider this a practical toolkit for regular security maintenance rather than a one-off checklist.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your practical work. First, you will clearly distinguish between automated vulnerability scanning and manual penetration testing so you know which approach fits your team and assets. Second, you will perform basic network discovery and port scanning with Nmap to build an accurate asset inventory for further analysis. Third, you will run or interpret scans produced by open-source tools such as OpenVAS/GVM, including configuring targets and tasks. Fourth, you will read a vulnerability report, understand CVSS severity, and prioritize remediation steps in context. Each objective ties a concrete skill to why it matters in operation: scanning finds likely issues; proper interpretation reduces noise and focuses scarce remediation time; and authorization prevents legal and operational damage. Throughout, you will learn safe defaults and common mistakes to avoid. By practicing these objectives in a lab, you’ll gain repeatable steps to keep systems accountable and auditable for compliance and security improvement.

screens.title: Scanning vs Pen Testing — Clear definitions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two terms you will use every day. A vulnerability scan is an automated pass that inspects hosts, services, and configurations against a maintained vulnerability database. It is non-intrusive by design, intended to provide broad coverage and repeatable baseline checks. For example, a weekly GVM scan can list packages with known CVEs and flag weak SSH ciphers. Penetration testing is different: it attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to determine whether an attacker can gain privilege or lateral movement. Pen tests are intrusive, time-limited, and often manual; they show realistic impact rather than just a list of matching signatures. As an LFCE you will mainly run and interpret vulnerability scans and coordinate pen tests with specialist teams. A common misconception is that a clean scan output means the system is secure. Scans only detect known issues and may miss chained exploits or logic flaws that a pen test would reveal. In practice use scans to maintain hygiene and reserve pen testing for high-value assets or after major changes. Which method to use depends on risk, cost, and the required level of assurance.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Scanning vs Pen Testing
Definitions and practical distinctions

Understand what each method promises, and what it cannot guarantee.

Vulnerability Scanning
  • Automated matching of system state to vulnerability signatures.
  • Non-intrusive, repeatable, suitable for scheduled checks.
  • Best for broad coverage and patch tracking.
Penetration Testing
  • Manual and automated techniques to attempt exploitation.
  • Intrusive and goal-oriented: demonstrates real impact.
  • Used for high assurance and attack-path analysis.
Concrete example
A weekly GVM scan flags outdated OpenSSH. A pen test attempts to exploit that outdated version chain to gain shell access and shows whether an exploit leads to privilege escalation.
Common mistake
Assuming scan results are complete. Scanners detect known patterns; they cannot always find chained or logic vulnerabilities a human tester might discover.
Key Takeaway

Use scans for routine hygiene and pen tests for validating exploitability and impact on critical systems.

Quick contrast
Scope
Scans: broad and regular. Pen tests: focused and time-bound.
Intrusiveness
Scans are generally non-intrusive; pen tests may intentionally disrupt to confirm exploitability.
Outcome
Scans: lists to prioritize. Pen tests: proof of concept and mitigation guidance.

screens.title: Nmap basics — Network discovery and port scanning
screens.narratorSegment: Nmap is the industry-standard tool for mapping a target network. Start with host discovery to confirm a target is reachable, then run a SYN scan to list open TCP ports. For example, a basic SYN scan uses the command written here visually: nmap -sS target_ip. That returns a list of ports in state open, closed, or filtered. To learn which services and versions are running, add service detection with -sV. For operating system guessing use -O, which examines TCP/IP stack fingerprints. An aggressive scan -A combines OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute; it is powerful but more intrusive and should only be used with explicit permission. A common mistake is using high timing options like -T5 on production systems; this can overload services or trigger alerts. In practice, begin with gentler scans and escalate if you have authorization and an agreed maintenance window. In the following code panel you will see example commands and a small simulated output to help you interpret results and plan remediation steps. Nmap basics — Network discovery and port scanning means use -ss for syn scans, -sv for service versions, -o for os detection, and -a for aggressive profiling; always get permission before aggressive scans.. In practical terms, essential commands to identify hosts, open ports, and services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Nmap Basics
Nmap command walkthrough

Commands you will use in the hands-on lab and what their output tells you.

nmap -sS <target_ip>
# SYN scan: lists open TCP ports without completing full connections

nmap -sV <target_ip>
# Service version detection: attempts to identify exact software versions

nmap -O <target_ip>
# OS detection: uses TCP/IP stack fingerprinting

nmap -A <target_ip>
# Aggressive: combines -O, -sV, script scanning, and traceroute; use with permission
Simulated output snippet
PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 7.4
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.6

OS guesses: Linux 3.x - 4.x
Interpretation
  • OpenSSH on 22 may need configuration hardening or patching.
  • Apache version disclosure suggests version hardening (suppress headers) and patch checks.
  • OS guess guides which packages to inspect for CVEs.
Best practices & caution
  • Obtain explicit written permission before scanning any asset you do not own.
  • Start with low-impact scans and increase scope slowly if authorized.
  • Avoid -T5 on production or sensitive systems to prevent service disruption.
Key Takeaway

Use Nmap methodically: discovery first, then targeted scans, and always respect authorization and system stability.

screens.title: Interpreting Nmap output — Practical examples
screens.narratorSegment: Reading Nmap output is a critical step between discovery and remediation. When Nmap reports an open port, you should note the port number, the service name, and the version string if available. For example, an open 22/tcp with OpenSSH 7.4 suggests checking if that OpenSSH release has known CVEs or weak defaults such as old MAC algorithms. An HTTP server that discloses a version in the Server header is an information disclosure finding; it may not itself allow remote code execution, but it helps attackers narrow their tools. OS detection provides a starting point for which package managers and kernel CVEs to check. Remember a common misconception: a filtered port doesn't mean the service is absent — it may be blocked by a firewall or IDS. Use additional targeted checks or authenticated scans to reduce uncertainty. In the lab, you will capture Nmap output and map each finding to a prioritized remediation step: update package, harden configuration, or schedule compensating controls. This disciplined translation from raw output to concrete remediation is what reduces risk quickly. Interpreting Nmap output — Practical examples means convert nmap findings into prioritized, actionable items: update software, harden configs, or schedule compensating controls based on exposure.. In practical terms, how to read open ports, services, and os guesses and turn them into actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Interpreting Nmap Output
From ports to remediation

Turn raw Nmap lines into concrete tasks and verifyable fixes.

# Example extraction from Nmap output
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 7.4
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.6

# Actions:
# - Check OpenSSH CVE history; harden MACs in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# - Remove version headers from Apache (ServerTokens Prod, ServerSignature Off)
# - Schedule patch and re-run targeted scan
Misconception
Filtered ports mean the service is blocked, not necessarily absent. Always combine findings with authenticated scans or host-level checks.
Concrete example
If Nmap reports Apache 2.4.6, verify package manager version and apply security updates, then re-scan to confirm removal of the vulnerable package.
Key Takeaway

Nmap output is a diagnostic. Use it to create verifiable remediation steps and follow up with authenticated checks or re-scans.

Quick checklist
  • Record port, service, and version strings for each finding.
  • Map each to package names or config files on the host.
  • Prioritize fixes and schedule a re-scan to verify the change.

screens.title: GVM / OpenVAS — Scan workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Greenbone Vulnerability Management, historically OpenVAS, gives you a full framework to manage vulnerability scans and reports. The workflow has four steps: define targets, configure scan tasks, run scans, and analyze reports. Defining targets means listing IPs or hostnames you are authorized to assess. Scan tasks let you choose scan templates—full and fast, host discovery, or authenticated scans if you have credentials. Authenticated scans require care: store and transmit credentials securely and limit their use to the scope and timeframe in your Rules of Engagement. After the scan completes, the report shows findings with severity and CVSS scores, descriptions, and suggested remediation steps. Interpreting the report involves looking beyond raw severity: consider exploitability, asset exposure, and business impact. For example, a high CVSS on a private management network may be lower priority than a public-facing service with a medium CVSS but easy exploitability. Finally, record actions and re-scan to ensure fixes are effective. That iterative loop—scan, remediate, verify—is essential for sustained security. GVM / OpenVAS — Scan workflow means define authorized targets, select scan templates, use authenticated scans when needed, analyze reports with cvss and context, then remediate and re-scan.. In practical terms, targets, scan tasks, authenticated checks, and report analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › GVM / OpenVAS Workflow
Scan workflow steps

A repeatable process reduces noise and increases verification confidence.

1. Define targets
List IPs/hosts and ensure explicit permission is recorded.
2. Configure task
Choose templates and authentication settings for deeper checks.
3. Run scan
Monitor performance and impact; avoid production disruption.
4. Analyze & remediate
Prioritize by CVSS, exploitability, and asset exposure; re-scan after fixes.
Authenticated scans
When you provide credentials the scanner can check installed packages and configuration files. This produces richer, more accurate findings but requires secure credential handling and approval in the rules of engagement.
Key Takeaway

Treat scanning as an iterative program: configure carefully, prioritize with context, and verify fixes with re-scans.

Report anatomy
  • Vulnerability title and description.
  • Severity and CVSS score.
  • Affected host and affected port/service.
  • Suggested remediation steps.

screens.title: CVSS and prioritization
screens.narratorSegment: CVSS, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, gives a numerical severity score for identified vulnerabilities. It is a standard helpful for comparing issues, but CVSS alone does not determine priority. When you read a report, start with CVSS to find critical and high items, but then ask three contextual questions: is the vulnerable service publicly accessible, how easy is the vulnerability to exploit, and what is the business impact if exploited? For instance, an SSH weak MAC algorithms finding with CVSS 7.5 is high because it can lead to data compromise; that often merits immediate remediation on public-facing systems. By contrast, a medium CVSS version disclosure on an internal service may be lower priority if the service is isolated. Prioritization should consider exploitability, available mitigations, and asset criticality. Always document the rationale for priority decisions and schedule re-scans after remediation to ensure the issue is resolved. This contextual approach prevents wasting time on low-risk items while missing serious exposure. CVSS and prioritization means use cvss as a starting point, then apply context—exposure, exploitability, and business impact—to choose remediation order.. In practical terms, how to read severity and place vulnerabilities in context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › CVSS & Prioritization
Reading CVSS with context

A numerical score helps triage, but do not treat it as the sole decision factor.

Three contextual checks
  1. Exposure: Is the service reachable from untrusted networks?
  2. Exploitability: Is a public exploit known and easy to run?
  3. Impact: Would exploitation affect critical business functions?
Example
SSH weak MACs (CVSS 7.5) on a public host is prioritized higher than an internal version disclosure with similar score because the public host has direct exposure and potential for data compromise.
Key Takeaway

Use CVSS to triage, then apply exposure and business impact to finalize remediation priority and schedule.

Prioritization matrix
High CVSS + Public = Urgent
Medium CVSS + Internal = Scheduled
Low CVSS + Isolated = Monitor

screens.title: Remediation and verification — scan → remediate → re-scan
screens.narratorSegment: Once you prioritize findings, the remediation stage begins. Start by mapping each vulnerability to an exact remediation action: update a package, change a configuration line, or implement a compensating control. For example, to fix weak SSH MAC algorithms edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and set a strong MACs directive, then restart the service. Create a change ticket that records the fix steps, the reason for the change, and the rollback plan. After applying the fix, re-scan the affected host or service to verify the vulnerability no longer appears. Documentation is essential: keep the original report, the remediation steps, the re-scan results, and the date of closure. This provides an audit trail for compliance and for future incident response. A common oversight is to assume a package update succeeded without verifying the scanner no longer reports the vulnerability. Re-scanning closes the loop and prevents the same finding from resurfacing in the next audit cycle. Remediation and verification — scan → remediate → re-scan means map vulnerabilities to exact fixes, document changes, and re-scan to confirm closure and maintain an auditable trail.. In practical terms, turn findings into change requests, apply fixes, and prove closure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Create a change ticket that records the fix steps, the reason for the change, and the rollback plan. After applying the fix, re-scan the affected host or service to verify the vulnerability no longer appears. Documentation is essential: keep the original report, the remediation steps, the re-scan results, and the date of closure. This provides an audit trail for compliance and for future incident response. A common oversight is to assume a package update succeeded without verifying the scanner no longer reports the vulnerability. Re-scanning closes the loop and prevents the same finding from resurfacing in the next audit cycle. Remediation and verification — scan → remediate → re-scan means map vulnerabilities to exact fixes, document changes, and re-scan to confirm closure and maintain an auditable trail.. In practical terms, turn findings into change requests, apply fixes, and prove closure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Remediation & Verification
From finding to closure

Documented changes and verification prevent recurring vulnerabilities and support audits.

# Example remediation for SSH weak MACs
# 1. Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config
#    Add: MACs hmac-sha2-512,hmac-sha2-256,umac-128@openssh.com

Verification
Run a focused scan against the updated service and archive the resulting report to prove closure.

A fix is not complete until you verify it with a re-scan and keep records of the remediation for audits.

screens.title: Ethical and legal considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Ethics and legality are core constraints for any testing activity. Always obtain explicit written permission that defines targets, permitted tests, timing, and contact persons before performing scans or pen tests. This document—often called Rules of Engagement—protects both the tester and the asset owner by clarifying expectations and potential impacts. Remember even non-intrusive scans can destabilize fragile systems, so communicate potential risks to stakeholders and schedule tests during agreed maintenance windows when necessary. Unauthorized testing can lead to legal penalties and unintended outages. As an LFCE you will often coordinate tests rather than act as the contracted pen tester; your role includes ensuring authorization, limiting scope, and documenting risk. A common misunderstanding is that internal corporate permission is always sufficient; in complex environments you may need sign-off from asset owners, network operators, and compliance teams. When in doubt, stop and confirm. Responsible testing preserves trust and prevents harm while delivering security improvements. Ethical and legal considerations means secure explicit written authorization with scope, timing, and contacts; communicate risks and avoid testing without clear permission.. Run these in your scanner VM against a target VM you control and have permission to test.

screens.title: Common scanner findings and how to act
screens.narratorSegment: Vulnerability scanners commonly report three classes of findings: outdated software versions, weak configurations, and information disclosure. Outdated software often maps directly to CVEs; the remediation is typically a package upgrade and related configuration checks. Weak configurations—such as weak SSH MAC algorithms—need targeted configuration changes followed by service restarts and verification. Information disclosure issues, like server version headers, are lower immediacy but useful for attackers; remedies include suppressing headers and removing unnecessary information. When you see many low-severity items, resist the urge to treat all as equal: prioritize based on exploitability and exposure. A practical example from the chapter shows SSH weak MACs as High (CVSS 7.5) and Apache version disclosure as Medium (CVSS 5.0). In most environments, fix the SSH configuration first, documenting the change and re-scanning to confirm the closure, then harden Apache. This approach prevents firefighting and focuses remediation where it most reduces risk. Common scanner findings and how to act means address outdated packages and weak configs first when exposed; treat version disclosure as supporting intelligence but lower immediate priority.. Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Common Findings & Actions
Examples and recommended actions

Use a prioritized approach rather than treating all findings equally.

Outdated software
Action: schedule package updates, confirm dependencies, and re-scan to ensure CVE closure.
Weak configuration
Action: apply secure config (e.g., SSH MACs), restart service, and document the change with verification evidence.
Information disclosure
Action: suppress extraneous headers, reduce visible version strings, and monitor for exploit attempts.
High vs Medium example
SSH weak MACs = High (address immediately on exposed hosts). Apache version disclosure = Medium (hardening and patch planning).
Decision guide
  1. Does the finding affect a public service? If yes, raise priority.
  2. Is a public exploit known? If yes, act quickly.
  3. Can you apply a quick mitigation (config change) to buy time? Use it.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two complementary practices that keep systems safe: vulnerability scanning and penetration testing. Vulnerability scanning is an automated sweep that compares hosts and services against a database of known issues so you can detect problems broadly and regularly. Penetration testing is an intentional, often manual, simulated attack that tries to exploit weaknesses to measure real-world impact. You will also learn core network discovery techniques with Nmap, and how to interpret a simulated OpenVAS, now Greenbone GVM, scan report. We will practice reading CVSS severity, prioritizing fixes, and documenting the scan-remediate-verify cycle. Importantly, we’ll cover the ethical and legal constraints that govern testing so you never scan without explicit written permission. By the end of this chapter you will know which tool to apply for which goal, how to run safe, sensible scans, and how to act on the results. Consider this a practical toolkit for regular security maintenance rather than a one-off checklist.

These learning objectives focus your practical work. First, you will clearly distinguish between automated vulnerability scanning and manual penetration testing so you know which approach fits your team and assets. Second, you will perform basic network discovery and port scanning with Nmap to build an accurate asset inventory for further analysis. Third, you will run or interpret scans produced by open-source tools such as OpenVAS/GVM, including configuring targets and tasks. Fourth, you will read a vulnerability report, understand CVSS severity, and prioritize remediation steps in context. Each objective ties a concrete skill to why it matters in operation: scanning finds likely issues; proper interpretation reduces noise and focuses scarce remediation time; and authorization prevents legal and operational damage. Throughout, you will learn safe defaults and common mistakes to avoid. By practicing these objectives in a lab, you’ll gain repeatable steps to keep systems accountable and auditable for compliance and security improvement.

These additional objectives expand the practical and ethical skills you need. First, you will perform authenticated scans with valid credentials to reveal deeper configuration issues that unauthenticated scans miss. Authenticated scanning provides more accurate results for installed software and patch status. Second, you will document the scan-remediate-verify cycle so every fix is auditable and re-tested. Third, you will apply prioritization heuristics: focus on public-facing critical services, outdated packages with known exploits, and weak configurations. Fourth, you will understand and prepare Rules of Engagement: define scope, timing, and contacts, and secure written permission before scanning. Ethics and legal awareness is not optional: unauthorized scanning can cause outages and legal exposure. These objectives emphasize reproducibility and safety so you can integrate vulnerability management into regular operations without causing harm to production systems.

Let's define the two terms you will use every day. A vulnerability scan is an automated pass that inspects hosts, services, and configurations against a maintained vulnerability database. It is non-intrusive by design, intended to provide broad coverage and repeatable baseline checks. For example, a weekly GVM scan can list packages with known CVEs and flag weak SSH ciphers. Penetration testing is different: it attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to determine whether an attacker can gain privilege or lateral movement. Pen tests are intrusive, time-limited, and often manual; they show realistic impact rather than just a list of matching signatures. As an LFCE you will mainly run and interpret vulnerability scans and coordinate pen tests with specialist teams. A common misconception is that a clean scan output means the system is secure. Scans only detect known issues and may miss chained exploits or logic flaws that a pen test would reveal. In practice use scans to maintain hygiene and reserve pen testing for high-value assets or after major changes. Which method to use depends on risk, cost, and the required level of assurance.

Nmap is the industry-standard tool for mapping a target network. Start with host discovery to confirm a target is reachable, then run a SYN scan to list open TCP ports. For example, a basic SYN scan uses the command written here visually: nmap -sS target_ip. That returns a list of ports in state open, closed, or filtered. To learn which services and versions are running, add service detection with -sV. For operating system guessing use -O, which examines TCP/IP stack fingerprints. An aggressive scan -A combines OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute; it is powerful but more intrusive and should only be used with explicit permission. A common mistake is using high timing options like -T5 on production systems; this can overload services or trigger alerts. In practice, begin with gentler scans and escalate if you have authorization and an agreed maintenance window. In the following code panel you will see example commands and a small simulated output to help you interpret results and plan remediation steps. Nmap basics — Network discovery and port scanning means use -ss for syn scans, -sv for service versions, -o for os detection, and -a for aggressive profiling; always get permission before aggressive scans.. In practical terms, essential commands to identify hosts, open ports, and services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading Nmap output is a critical step between discovery and remediation. When Nmap reports an open port, you should note the port number, the service name, and the version string if available. For example, an open 22/tcp with OpenSSH 7.4 suggests checking if that OpenSSH release has known CVEs or weak defaults such as old MAC algorithms. An HTTP server that discloses a version in the Server header is an information disclosure finding; it may not itself allow remote code execution, but it helps attackers narrow their tools. OS detection provides a starting point for which package managers and kernel CVEs to check. Remember a common misconception: a filtered port doesn't mean the service is absent — it may be blocked by a firewall or IDS. Use additional targeted checks or authenticated scans to reduce uncertainty. In the lab, you will capture Nmap output and map each finding to a prioritized remediation step: update package, harden configuration, or schedule compensating controls. This disciplined translation from raw output to concrete remediation is what reduces risk quickly. Interpreting Nmap output — Practical examples means convert nmap findings into prioritized, actionable items: update software, harden configs, or schedule compensating controls based on exposure.. In practical terms, how to read open ports, services, and os guesses and turn them into actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Greenbone Vulnerability Management, historically OpenVAS, gives you a full framework to manage vulnerability scans and reports. The workflow has four steps: define targets, configure scan tasks, run scans, and analyze reports. Defining targets means listing IPs or hostnames you are authorized to assess. Scan tasks let you choose scan templates—full and fast, host discovery, or authenticated scans if you have credentials. Authenticated scans require care: store and transmit credentials securely and limit their use to the scope and timeframe in your Rules of Engagement. After the scan completes, the report shows findings with severity and CVSS scores, descriptions, and suggested remediation steps. Interpreting the report involves looking beyond raw severity: consider exploitability, asset exposure, and business impact. For example, a high CVSS on a private management network may be lower priority than a public-facing service with a medium CVSS but easy exploitability. Finally, record actions and re-scan to ensure fixes are effective. That iterative loop—scan, remediate, verify—is essential for sustained security. GVM / OpenVAS — Scan workflow means define authorized targets, select scan templates, use authenticated scans when needed, analyze reports with cvss and context, then remediate and re-scan.. In practical terms, targets, scan tasks, authenticated checks, and report analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CVSS, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, gives a numerical severity score for identified vulnerabilities. It is a standard helpful for comparing issues, but CVSS alone does not determine priority. When you read a report, start with CVSS to find critical and high items, but then ask three contextual questions: is the vulnerable service publicly accessible, how easy is the vulnerability to exploit, and what is the business impact if exploited? For instance, an SSH weak MAC algorithms finding with CVSS 7.5 is high because it can lead to data compromise; that often merits immediate remediation on public-facing systems. By contrast, a medium CVSS version disclosure on an internal service may be lower priority if the service is isolated. Prioritization should consider exploitability, available mitigations, and asset criticality. Always document the rationale for priority decisions and schedule re-scans after remediation to ensure the issue is resolved. This contextual approach prevents wasting time on low-risk items while missing serious exposure. CVSS and prioritization means use cvss as a starting point, then apply context—exposure, exploitability, and business impact—to choose remediation order.. In practical terms, how to read severity and place vulnerabilities in context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Once you prioritize findings, the remediation stage begins. Start by mapping each vulnerability to an exact remediation action: update a package, change a configuration line, or implement a compensating control. For example, to fix weak SSH MAC algorithms edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and set a strong MACs directive, then restart the service. Create a change ticket that records the fix steps, the reason for the change, and the rollback plan. Ethics and legality are core constraints for any testing activity. Always obtain explicit written permission that defines targets, permitted tests, timing, and contact persons before performing scans or pen tests. This document—often called Rules of Engagement—protects both the tester and the asset owner by clarifying expectations and potential impacts. Remember even non-intrusive scans can destabilize fragile systems, so communicate potential risks to stakeholders and schedule tests during agreed maintenance windows when necessary. Unauthorized testing can lead to legal penalties and unintended outages. As an LFCE you will often coordinate tests rather than act as the contracted pen tester; your role includes ensuring authorization, limiting scope, and documenting risk. A common misunderstanding is that internal corporate permission is always sufficient; in complex environments you may need sign-off from asset owners, network operators, and compliance teams. Vulnerability scanners commonly report three classes of findings: outdated software versions, weak configurations, and information disclosure. Outdated software often maps directly to CVEs; the remediation is typically a package upgrade and related configuration checks. Weak configurations—such as weak SSH MAC algorithms—need targeted configuration changes followed by service restarts and verification. Information disclosure issues, like server version headers, are lower immediacy but useful for attackers; remedies include suppressing headers and removing unnecessary information. When you see many low-severity items, resist the urge to treat all as equal: prioritize based on exploitability and exposure. A practical example from the chapter shows SSH weak MACs as High (CVSS 7.5) and Apache version disclosure as Medium (CVSS 5.0). In most environments, fix the SSH configuration first, documenting the change and re-scanning to confirm the closure, then harden Apache. This approach prevents firefighting and focuses remediation where it most reduces risk. Keep these concise ideas in mind. First, vulnerability scanning is an automated, repeatable process for finding known issues and should be part of routine system hygiene. Second, penetration testing simulates real attacks and is used to validate exploitability and impact; it is complementary to scanning and usually more intrusive. Third, Nmap remains a core discovery tool: -sS for SYN scans, -sV for service versions, -O for OS detection, and -A for aggressive profiling when authorized. These concepts form the foundation of a pragmatic vulnerability management program where scanning informs prioritized remediation and pen tests validate critical scenarios.
